concepts.name: Function
concepts.statement: A function f consists of a set of inputs, a set of outputs, and a rule for assigning each input to exactly one output. When we know the input, the output is determined, so we say that the output is a function of the input.

concepts.name: Domain
concepts.statement: The domain of a function is its set of inputs. Where a function is given by an equation and no domain is stated, the domain is taken to be the set of all real numbers x for which f(x) is a real number.

concepts.name: Range
concepts.statement: The range of a function is its set of outputs: every value f(x) takes as x runs over the domain.

concepts.name: Independent variable
concepts.statement: For a function y = f(x), the input x is the independent variable.

concepts.name: Dependent variable
concepts.statement: For a function y = f(x), the output y is the dependent variable, because it depends on the input x.

concepts.name: Graph of a function
concepts.statement: The graph of a function f is the set of all points (x, y) in the coordinate plane such that x is in the domain of f and y = f(x).

concepts.name: Interval notation
concepts.statement: A set of real numbers can be described in set-builder notation, {x | x has some property}, or, when it holds every number between two endpoints, in interval notation: (a, b) leaves both endpoints out, [a, b] includes them, and ∞ and −∞, which are not real numbers, mark a side with no end.

concepts.name: Natural domain
concepts.statement: The natural domain of a function given by a formula is the set of all real numbers for which the formula gives a real output; the natural domain of f(x) = √x is the set of nonnegative real numbers.

concepts.name: Piecewise-defined function
concepts.statement: A piecewise-defined function is defined by different equations on different parts of its domain; which equation gives f(x) depends on the part of the domain in which x falls.

concepts.name: Table of values
concepts.statement: A table of values lists inputs of a function and their corresponding outputs.

concepts.name: Zeros of a function
concepts.statement: The zeros of a function f are the values of x where f(x) = 0; they are where the graph of f intersects the x-axis. A function may have any number of zeros.

concepts.name: y-intercept
concepts.statement: The y-intercept of a function f, if it exists, is the point (0, f(0)). A function has exactly one y-intercept if 0 is in its domain and none otherwise.

concepts.name: Vertical line test
concepts.statement: Given a function f, every vertical line that may be drawn intersects the graph of f no more than once. If any vertical line intersects a set of points more than once, the set of points does not represent a function.

concepts.name: Increasing on an interval
concepts.statement: A function f is increasing on the interval I if f(x₁) ≤ f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂ in I, and strictly increasing there if f(x₁) < f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂.

concepts.name: Decreasing on an interval
concepts.statement: A function f is decreasing on the interval I if f(x₁) ≥ f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂ in I, and strictly decreasing there if f(x₁) > f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂.

concepts.name: Combinations of functions
concepts.statement: Given two functions f and g, we can define four new functions by writing them with an operator: their sum, difference, product and quotient, the quotient only where g(x) ≠ 0. Each is defined where both f and g are.

concepts.name: Composite function
concepts.statement: If f has domain A and range B, g has domain D, and B is a subset of D, the composite function g ∘ f is the function with domain A such that (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)): f maps x to f(x), and g maps f(x) on to g(f(x)). The order in which we compose functions matters.

concepts.name: Symmetry about the y-axis
concepts.statement: The graph of a function f is symmetric about the y-axis if (−x, y) is on the graph whenever (x, y) is: the part of the curve to the right of the y-axis, flipped over it, lies exactly on the part to the left.

concepts.name: Symmetry about the origin
concepts.statement: The graph of a function f is symmetric about the origin if (−x, −y) is on the graph whenever (x, y) is: rotated 180° about the origin, the graph looks exactly the same.

concepts.name: Even function
concepts.statement: A function f is even if f(−x) = f(x) for all x in its domain. An even function is symmetric about the y-axis.

concepts.name: Odd function
concepts.statement: A function f is odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for all x in its domain. An odd function is symmetric about the origin.

concepts.name: Absolute value function
concepts.statement: The absolute value function |x| is −x for x < 0 and x for x ≥ 0. Its output is positive for every nonzero input and 0 at x = 0, so its range is {y | y ≥ 0}; it is symmetric about the y-axis and so even.

concepts.name: Slope
concepts.statement: The slope of a line through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = Δy/Δx, the change in y for each unit change in x. For a line it does not depend on which two points are chosen.

concepts.name: Linear function
concepts.statement: A linear function is one that can be written in the form f(x) = mx + b; its graph is a line with slope m.

concepts.name: Point-slope equation
concepts.statement: The point-slope equation of the line through (x₁, y₁) with slope m is y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

concepts.name: Slope-intercept form
concepts.statement: The equation of the line with slope m and y-intercept (0, b) in slope-intercept form is y = mx + b.

concepts.name: Standard form of a line
concepts.statement: The standard form of a line is ax + by = c, where a and b are not both zero; it is more general than the other forms because it allows a vertical line, x = k.

concepts.name: Polynomial function
concepts.statement: A polynomial function is any function that can be written as f(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁x + a₀ for some integer n ≥ 0 and constants aₙ, …, a₀ with aₙ ≠ 0; if every coefficient is 0 it is the zero function.

concepts.name: Degree
concepts.statement: The degree of a polynomial function is the value n of the largest exponent of any of its terms.

concepts.name: Leading coefficient
concepts.statement: The leading coefficient of a polynomial of degree n is the constant aₙ that multiplies xⁿ.

concepts.name: Constant function
concepts.statement: A polynomial of degree 0, f(x) = a₀, is a constant function; its graph is a horizontal line.

concepts.name: Quadratic function
concepts.statement: A quadratic function is a polynomial of degree 2, f(x) = ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0; its graph is a parabola, opening upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0.

concepts.name: Cubic function
concepts.statement: A cubic function is a polynomial of degree 3, f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d with a ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Power function
concepts.statement: A power function is any function of the form f(x) = axᵇ, where a and b are real numbers. When the exponent is a positive integer n, axⁿ is a polynomial, even if n is even and odd if n is odd.

concepts.name: End behavior of a polynomial
concepts.statement: The end behavior of a function is what happens to f(x) as x → ∞ and as x → −∞. A polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 satisfies f(x) → ±∞ as x → ±∞, and its leading term decides which: the sign of the leading coefficient and whether n is even or odd.

concepts.name: Quadratic formula
concepts.statement: The solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 are x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). If the discriminant b² − 4ac is positive there are two real solutions, if it is zero there is one, and if it is negative there is none.

concepts.name: Mathematical model
concepts.statement: A mathematical model is a method of simulating a real-life situation with mathematical equations, such as a function fitted to collected data.

concepts.name: Algebraic function
concepts.statement: An algebraic function is one that involves only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, rational powers and roots applied to the input variable x.

concepts.name: Rational function
concepts.statement: A rational function is a quotient of polynomials, f(x) = p(x)/q(x); its domain is the set of x with q(x) ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Root function
concepts.statement: A root function is a power function f(x) = x^{1/n} for an integer n ≥ 2. Its domain is [0, ∞) if n is even and (−∞, ∞) if n is odd, and for odd n it is an odd function.

concepts.name: Transcendental function
concepts.statement: A transcendental function is one that cannot be described by basic algebraic operations; the most common are the trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions.

concepts.name: Exponential function
concepts.statement: An exponential function is a function of the form f(x) = bˣ, where the base b > 0 and b ≠ 1. It is increasing if b > 1 and decreasing if 0 < b < 1, with domain (−∞, ∞) and range (0, ∞).

concepts.name: Logarithmic function
concepts.statement: A logarithmic function is a function f(x) = log_b(x) for some base b > 0, b ≠ 1, where log_b(x) = y if and only if bʸ = x. It is the inverse of y = bˣ, with domain (0, ∞) and range (−∞, ∞).

concepts.name: Transformation of a function
concepts.statement: A transformation of a function is a shift, scaling or reflection of its graph: f(x) + c shifts it up c units, f(x + c) left c units, cf(x) scales it vertically and f(cx) horizontally by a factor of c, and −f(x) and f(−x) reflect it about the x- and y-axes. The graph of y = cf(a(x + b)) + d comes from that of y = f(x) by the horizontal shift, the horizontal scaling, the vertical scaling and the vertical shift, in that order.

concepts.name: Radian
concepts.statement: The radian measure of an angle θ is the length s of the arc it cuts off on the unit circle, so the angle of an arc of length 1 has radian measure 1. An angle of 180° has a radian measure of π rad.

concepts.name: Trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: For a point P = (x, y) on the unit circle and the angle θ from the positive x-axis to OP, sin θ = y, cos θ = x, tan θ = y/x, csc θ = 1/y, sec θ = 1/x and cot θ = x/y, wherever the quotient is defined. On a circle of radius r they are the same ratios with x/r and y/r, and for an acute angle they are ratios of two sides of a right triangle.

concepts.name: Trigonometric identity
concepts.statement: A trigonometric identity is an equation involving trigonometric functions that is true for all angles θ for which the functions in it are defined.

concepts.name: Reciprocal and ratio identities
concepts.statement: The cotangent, cosecant and secant are the reciprocals of the tangent, sine and cosine, and the tangent and cotangent are the ratios of sine and cosine.

concepts.name: Pythagorean identities
concepts.statement: For every angle θ where the functions are defined, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

concepts.name: Addition and subtraction formulas
concepts.statement: The sine and cosine of a sum or difference of two angles are given by the sines and cosines of the angles.

concepts.name: Double-angle formulas
concepts.statement: The sine and cosine of twice an angle: sin(2θ) = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos(2θ) = 2cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2sin²θ = cos²θ − sin²θ.

concepts.name: Periodic function
concepts.statement: A function is periodic if it has a repeating pattern as the values of x move from left to right. The trigonometric functions are periodic, since θ and θ + 2π correspond to the same point of the unit circle.

concepts.name: Period
concepts.statement: The period of a function f is the smallest positive value p such that f(x + p) = f(x) for all x in its domain. Sine, cosine, secant and cosecant have period 2π; tangent and cotangent have period π.

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.statement: For a transformed sine or cosine f(x) = A sin(B(x − α)) + C, the factor A stretches the graph vertically by |A|, and |A| is called the amplitude of f.

concepts.name: Generalized sine function
concepts.statement: A transformed sine function f(x) = A sin(B(x − α)) + C has amplitude |A| and period 2π/|B|; α shifts its graph horizontally, a phase shift, and C shifts it vertically. A cosine is a sine shifted left π/2 units.

concepts.name: One-to-one function
concepts.statement: A function f is one-to-one if f(x₁) ≠ f(x₂) when x₁ ≠ x₂: no two inputs are sent to the same output.

concepts.name: Inverse function
concepts.statement: Given a function f with domain D and range R, its inverse function, if it exists, is the function f⁻¹ with domain R and range D such that f⁻¹(y) = x if f(x) = y. A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one.

concepts.name: Horizontal line test
concepts.statement: A function f is one-to-one if and only if every horizontal line intersects the graph of f no more than once.

concepts.name: Finding an inverse function
concepts.statement: To find the inverse of a one-to-one function, solve the equation y = f(x) for x, then interchange the variables x and y and write y = f⁻¹(x).

concepts.name: Graph of an inverse function
concepts.statement: If (a, b) is on the graph of f, then (b, a) is on the graph of f⁻¹, so the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f about the line y = x.

concepts.name: Restricted domain
concepts.statement: A restricted domain is a subset of the domain of a function. A function that is not one-to-one can be restricted to a smaller domain on which it is, and its inverse defined there.

concepts.name: Inverse trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: The inverse trigonometric functions are the inverses of the trigonometric functions on restricted domains where they are one-to-one: sin⁻¹ x = y if sin y = x and −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, cos⁻¹ x = y if cos y = x and 0 ≤ y ≤ π, both for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1, and similarly for tan⁻¹, cot⁻¹, csc⁻¹ and sec⁻¹.

concepts.name: Base
concepts.statement: The base is the number b in the exponential function f(x) = bˣ and the logarithmic function f(x) = log_b x.

concepts.name: Exponent
concepts.statement: The exponent is the value x in the expression bˣ.

concepts.name: Laws of exponents
concepts.statement: For any constants a > 0, b > 0 and all x and y: bˣ·bʸ = bˣ⁺ʸ, bˣ/bʸ = bˣ⁻ʸ, (bˣ)ʸ = bˣʸ, (ab)ˣ = aˣbˣ and aˣ/bˣ = (a/b)ˣ.

concepts.name: Compound interest
concepts.statement: P dollars invested at an annual interest rate r, compounded n times per year, grow to A(t) = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ after t years; compounded continuously, to A(t) = Pe^{rt}.

concepts.name: The number e
concepts.statement: As m gets larger, the quantity (1 + 1/m)ᵐ gets closer to some real number, and we define that number to be e; to six decimal places, e ≈ 2.718282.

concepts.name: Natural exponential function
concepts.statement: The natural exponential function is f(x) = eˣ, the exponential function with base e. It is the only exponential function whose tangent line at x = 0 has slope 1.

concepts.name: Natural logarithm
concepts.statement: The natural logarithm is the logarithm with base e, ln x = log_e x, the inverse of the natural exponential function: ln(eˣ) = x for all x and e^{ln x} = x for x > 0.

concepts.name: Common logarithm
concepts.statement: The common logarithm is the logarithm with base 10, written log₁₀ or log.

concepts.name: Properties of logarithms
concepts.statement: If a, b, c > 0, b ≠ 1, and r is any real number, then log_b(ac) = log_b(a) + log_b(c), log_b(a/c) = log_b(a) − log_b(c) and log_b(aʳ) = r log_b(a): the product, quotient and power properties.

concepts.name: Change-of-base formulas
concepts.statement: For a > 0, b > 0, a ≠ 1 and b ≠ 1, aˣ = b^{x log_b a} for any real x and log_a x = log_b x / log_b a for x > 0, so an exponential or logarithmic function in any base can be written in base e.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: The hyperbolic functions sinh, cosh, tanh, csch, sech and coth involve combinations of eˣ and e⁻ˣ: cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2 and sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, and the other four are their quotients and reciprocals.

concepts.name: Identities involving hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: The hyperbolic functions satisfy identities like the trigonometric ones: cosh is even and sinh odd, cosh x ± sinh x = e^{±x}, cosh²x − sinh²x = 1, and sums of arguments expand as for sine and cosine.

concepts.name: Inverse hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: The inverse hyperbolic functions are the inverses of the hyperbolic functions, cosh and sech restricted to [0, ∞); each can be written as a composition of the natural logarithm and an algebraic function.

concepts.name: Rate of change
concepts.statement: The rate of change of a function measures how fast its values change as its input changes; for a linear function it is constant and given by the slope, but no single number gives it for a nonlinear function.

concepts.name: Secant
concepts.statement: The secant to the function f(x) through the points (a, f(a)) and (x, f(x)) is the line passing through these points; its slope estimates the rate of change of f at a, and the estimate improves as x gets closer to a.

concepts.name: Tangent
concepts.statement: A tangent line to the graph of a function at a point (a, f(a)) is the line that secant lines through (a, f(a)) approach as they are taken through points on the function with x-values that approach a; its slope measures the rate of change of the function at a, the derivative f′(a).

concepts.name: Tangent problem
concepts.statement: The tangent problem asks how to determine the slope of a line tangent to a curve at a point; it is solved by letting x approach a in the slope of the secant line, and it led to differential calculus.

concepts.name: Differential calculus
concepts.statement: Differential calculus is the field of calculus concerned with the study of derivatives and their applications.

concepts.name: Average velocity
concepts.statement: The average velocity of an object over a time period is the change in its position divided by the length of the time period: for a position s(t), over [a, t] it is (s(t) − s(a))/(t − a), the slope of a secant line to s.

concepts.name: Limit
concepts.statement: Letting x or t approach a in an expression is called taking a limit; the limit of a function f(x) as x approaches a is the value that f(x) approaches as x approaches a.

concepts.name: Instantaneous velocity
concepts.statement: For a position function s(t), the instantaneous velocity at a time t = a is the value that the average velocities approach on intervals of the form [a, t] and [t, a] as the values of t become closer to a, provided such a value exists.

concepts.name: Area problem
concepts.statement: The area problem asks how to find the area between the graph of a function and the x-axis over an interval [a, b]; the area is approximated by the sum of the areas of thin rectangles, and as their widths approach zero the sums approach the area, a limit that underlies the definite integral.

concepts.name: Integral calculus
concepts.statement: Integral calculus is the study of integrals and their applications.

concepts.name: Multivariable calculus
concepts.statement: Multivariable calculus is the study of the calculus of functions of two or more variables, such as motion in space and the volumes of solids under surfaces.

concepts.name: Intuitive definition of the limit
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be defined at all values in an open interval containing a, with the possible exception of a itself, and let L be a real number. If all values of f(x) approach L as the values of x (≠ a) approach a, then the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L: as x gets closer to a, f(x) gets closer and stays close to L.

concepts.name: Evaluating a limit with a table
concepts.statement: To estimate the limit of f(x) as x approaches a, make a table of functional values for x approaching a from below and from above (a ± 0.1, a ± 0.01, …); if both columns approach a common value L, the limit is L, which a graph traced near a can confirm.

concepts.name: Two important limits
concepts.statement: For a real number a and a constant c, the limit of x as x approaches a is a, and the limit of the constant c is c.

concepts.name: Existence of a limit
concepts.statement: For the limit of a function to exist at a point, the functional values must approach a single real number there; if they do not, the limit does not exist (DNE), as for sin(1/x) as x approaches 0.

concepts.name: One-sided limit
concepts.statement: A one-sided limit is a limit taken from either the left or the right: L is the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left if the values f(x) approach L as x < a approaches a, and from the right if they approach L as x > a approaches a.

concepts.name: Relating one-sided and two-sided limits
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be defined at all values in an open interval containing a, with the possible exception of a, and let L be a real number. Then the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L if and only if the limits from the left and from the right are both L.

forms.latex: \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\;\text{if and only if}\;\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L\;\text{and}\;\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L

concepts.name: Infinite limit
concepts.statement: A function has an infinite limit at a point a if its values increase or decrease without bound as x approaches a, from the left, from the right or from both sides; writing that the limit is +∞ or −∞ describes this behavior and does not assert that a limit exists.

concepts.name: Infinite limits from positive integers
concepts.statement: For a positive integer n, 1/(x − a)ⁿ has an infinite limit at a: +∞ from both sides if n is even; +∞ from the right and −∞ from the left if n is odd.

concepts.name: Vertical asymptote
concepts.statement: The line x = a is a vertical asymptote of f(x) if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left, from the right or from both sides is +∞ or −∞.

concepts.name: Sum law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits: L + M.

concepts.name: Difference law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits: L − M.

concepts.name: Constant multiple law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a constant c times a function is c times its limit: cL.

concepts.name: Product law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a product is the product of the limits: L · M.

concepts.name: Quotient law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, L/M, provided M ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Power law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of the nth power of a function is the nth power of its limit, Lⁿ, for every positive integer n.

concepts.name: Root law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of the nth root of a function is the nth root of its limit, for all L if n is odd and for L ≥ 0 if n is even and f(x) ≥ 0.

concepts.name: Limit laws
concepts.statement: The limit laws are the individual properties of limits: for f(x) and g(x) defined for all x ≠ a over some open interval containing a, with limits L and M at a, and a constant c, the limit of a sum, difference, constant multiple, product, quotient (M ≠ 0), power or root is that combination of L and M.

concepts.name: Limits of polynomial and rational functions
concepts.statement: For polynomials p(x) and q(x) and a real number a, the limit of p(x) as x approaches a is p(a), and the limit of p(x)/q(x) is p(a)/q(a) when q(a) ≠ 0: such limits are found by direct substitution.

concepts.name: Limits of functions equal near a
concepts.statement: If f(x) = g(x) for all x ≠ a over some open interval containing a, then the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are equal.

concepts.name: Indeterminate form 0/0
concepts.statement: A limit of f(x)/g(x) as x approaches a where the limits of f(x) and g(x) are both 0 has the indeterminate form 0/0: substitution gives no value, and the limit may still exist.

concepts.name: Evaluating a 0/0 limit
concepts.statement: To evaluate a limit of f(x)/g(x) with the indeterminate form 0/0, find a function equal to it for all x ≠ a near a, by factoring and canceling, multiplying by a conjugate where a square root is involved, or simplifying a complex fraction, then apply the limit laws.

concepts.name: Squeeze theorem
concepts.statement: Let f(x), g(x) and h(x) be defined for all x ≠ a over an open interval containing a. If f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) for all x ≠ a in that interval and the limits of f(x) and h(x) as x approaches a are both the real number L, then the limit of g(x) is L.

concepts.name: Important trigonometric limits
concepts.statement: As θ approaches 0, sin θ approaches 0, cos θ approaches 1, sin θ/θ approaches 1 and (1 − cos θ)/θ approaches 0; the squeeze theorem on the unit circle, where sin θ < θ < tan θ for 0 < θ < π/2, establishes them.

concepts.name: Continuity at a point
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is continuous at a point a if and only if f(a) is defined, the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists, and that limit equals f(a); intuitively, its graph has no break at a.

concepts.name: Discontinuity at a point
concepts.statement: A function is discontinuous at a point, or has a discontinuity at the point, if it is not continuous there.

concepts.name: Determining continuity at a point
concepts.statement: To decide whether f is continuous at a: check that f(a) is defined; compute the limit of f(x) as x approaches a, through the one-sided limits if needed, and check that it exists; compare it with f(a). A failure at any step means f is not continuous at a.

concepts.name: Continuity of polynomials and rational functions
concepts.statement: Polynomials and rational functions are continuous at every point in their domains.

concepts.name: Removable discontinuity
concepts.statement: A function f discontinuous at a has a removable discontinuity at a if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists; its graph has a hole there.

concepts.name: Jump discontinuity
concepts.statement: A function f discontinuous at a has a jump discontinuity at a if the limits of f(x) from the left and from the right both exist as real numbers but are not equal.

concepts.name: Infinite discontinuity
concepts.statement: A function f discontinuous at a has an infinite discontinuity at a if its limit from the left or from the right is +∞ or −∞; it lies at a vertical asymptote.

concepts.name: Continuity from the right
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is continuous from the right at a if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the right is f(a).

concepts.name: Continuity from the left
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is continuous from the left at a if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left is f(a).

concepts.name: Continuity over an interval
concepts.statement: A function is continuous over an open interval if it is continuous at every point in it, and over a closed interval [a, b] if it is continuous at every point of (a, b), continuous from the right at a and from the left at b; its graph can then be traced without lifting the pencil.

concepts.name: Composite function theorem
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous at L and the limit of g(x) as x approaches a is L, then the limit of f(g(x)) as x approaches a is f(L).

concepts.name: Continuity of trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: Trigonometric functions are continuous over their entire domains.

concepts.name: Intermediate Value Theorem
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over a closed, bounded interval [a, b]. If z is any real number between f(a) and f(b), then there is a number c in [a, b] satisfying f(c) = z.

concepts.name: Epsilon-delta definition of the limit
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be defined for all x ≠ a over an open interval containing a, and let L be a real number. Then the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L if, for every ε > 0, there exists a δ > 0 such that if 0 < |x − a| < δ, then |f(x) − L| < ε.

concepts.name: Proving a limit with epsilon and delta
concepts.statement: To prove that the limit of a specific f(x) as x approaches a is L: let ε > 0; choose δ, found algebraically or geometrically from |f(x) − L| < ε; assume 0 < |x − a| < δ; use it to show |f(x) − L| < ε; conclude that the limit is L.

concepts.name: Triangle inequality
concepts.statement: The triangle inequality states that if a and b are any real numbers, then |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.

concepts.name: A limit that does not exist
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a does not exist if for every real number L there exists ε > 0 so that for all δ > 0 there is an x satisfying 0 < |x − a| < δ with |f(x) − L| ≥ ε.

concepts.name: Epsilon-delta one-sided limits
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the right is L if for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that 0 < x − a < δ implies |f(x) − L| < ε; from the left, −δ < x − a < 0 replaces 0 < x − a < δ.

concepts.name: Epsilon-delta infinite limits
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a is +∞ if for every M > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ implies f(x) > M, and −∞ if it implies f(x) < −M.

concepts.name: Difference quotient
concepts.statement: For a function f defined on an interval I containing a, the difference quotient (f(x) − f(a))/(x − a), for x ≠ a in I, is the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (x, f(x)); with increment h ≠ 0 it is (f(a + h) − f(a))/h.

concepts.name: Slope of the tangent line
concepts.statement: For a function f defined in an open interval containing a, the tangent line to f at a is the line through (a, f(a)) whose slope m_tan is the limit of the difference quotient as x approaches a, or as h approaches 0, provided this limit exists.

concepts.name: Local linearity
concepts.statement: In a series of tighter intervals about a, the graph of a function and its tangent line at a appear to coincide, so the values on the tangent line approximate the function near a: the graph is locally linear there.

concepts.name: Finding the equation of a tangent line
concepts.statement: To find an equation of the line tangent to the graph of f at x = a, find its slope from the limit of the difference quotient, find the point (a, f(a)) it passes through, and write the line with the point-slope equation.

concepts.name: Derivative
concepts.statement: The derivative of a function f(x) at a, denoted f′(a), is the limit of the difference quotient as x approaches a, or of the difference quotient with increment h as h approaches 0, provided this limit exists: the slope of the tangent line to the function at a.

concepts.name: Differentiation
concepts.statement: Differentiation is the process of finding a derivative.

concepts.name: Estimating a derivative from a table
concepts.statement: To estimate f′(a), tabulate the difference quotient for values of x just below and just above a, or for small positive and negative h, and read off the value the quotients approach.

concepts.name: Instantaneous rate of change
concepts.statement: The instantaneous rate of change of a function f(x) at a value a is its derivative f′(a).

concepts.name: Derivative function
concepts.statement: The derivative function of f, denoted f′, is the function whose domain consists of those values of x for which the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x))/h as h approaches 0 exists, and whose value there is that limit; it gives the derivative of f at each such point.

concepts.name: Differentiable at a point
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is differentiable at a if f′(a) exists.

concepts.name: Differentiable on a set
concepts.statement: A function is differentiable on S if it is differentiable at every point in an open set S.

concepts.name: Differentiable function
concepts.statement: A differentiable function is one for which f′(x) exists on its domain.

concepts.name: Leibniz notation
concepts.statement: For y = f(x) the derivative may be written f′(x), dy/dx, y′ or d/dx(f(x)); in Leibniz notation dy/dx is the limit of the secant slopes Δy/Δx as Δx approaches 0, the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x.

concepts.name: Graph of the derivative
concepts.statement: The graph of f′ follows the graph of f: where f has a tangent line with positive slope, f′(x) > 0; where the slope is negative, f′(x) < 0; where f has a horizontal tangent line, f′(x) = 0.

concepts.name: Sketching a derivative from a graph
concepts.statement: To sketch f′ from the graph of f, mark where f has horizontal tangents (zeros of f′), where f increases (f′ above the axis) and decreases (below), and how steeply, and draw a curve through these.

concepts.name: Differentiability implies continuity
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be a function and a be in its domain. If f(x) is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a; a function that is continuous at a point need not be differentiable there.

concepts.name: Where a function fails to be differentiable
concepts.statement: A function is not differentiable at a point if it is not continuous there, if its graph has a sharp corner or cusp there, where the one-sided limits of the secant slopes differ, if it has a vertical tangent line there, or in more complicated ways, as when the secant slopes oscillate.

concepts.name: Higher-order derivative
concepts.statement: The derivative of a derivative is the second derivative, and continuing gives the third, fourth and nth derivatives; collectively these are the higher-order derivatives, written f″(x), f‴(x), f⁽⁴⁾(x), …, f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) or d²y/dx², d³y/dx³, …, dⁿy/dxⁿ.

concepts.name: Constant rule
concepts.statement: The derivative of a constant function is zero: if f(x) = c for a constant c, then f′(x) = 0.

concepts.name: Power rule
concepts.statement: Let n be a positive integer. If f(x) = xⁿ, then f′(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹: the power on x becomes the coefficient and the power on x in the derivative decreases by 1.

concepts.name: Sum rule
concepts.statement: The derivative of the sum of a function f and a function g is the sum of the derivative of f and the derivative of g.

concepts.name: Difference rule
concepts.statement: The derivative of the difference of a function f and a function g is the difference of the derivative of f and the derivative of g.

concepts.name: Constant multiple rule
concepts.statement: The derivative of a constant k multiplied by a function f is the constant multiplied by the derivative of f.

concepts.name: Product rule
concepts.statement: For differentiable functions f(x) and g(x), the derivative of the product is the derivative of the first function times the second function plus the derivative of the second function times the first function.

concepts.name: Quotient rule
concepts.statement: For differentiable functions f(x) and g(x), the derivative of the quotient f(x)/g(x) is the derivative of the numerator times the denominator minus the derivative of the denominator times the numerator, all divided by the square of the denominator.

concepts.name: Extended power rule
concepts.statement: If k is a negative integer, then the derivative of xᵏ is kxᵏ⁻¹, so the power rule holds for negative integer powers too.

concepts.name: Combining differentiation rules
concepts.statement: By combining the differentiation rules we may find the derivative of any polynomial or rational function; a good rule of thumb is to apply the rules in reverse of the order in which we would evaluate the function.

concepts.name: Amount of change
concepts.statement: The amount of change of a function f(x) over an interval [a, a + h] is the change in its y-values over that interval, f(a + h) − f(a).

concepts.name: Average rate of change
concepts.statement: The average rate of change of a function f over an interval [a, a + h] is the ratio of the amount of change over the interval to the corresponding change in the x-values, (f(a + h) − f(a))/h.

concepts.name: Amount of change formula
concepts.statement: For small enough h, f′(a) ≈ (f(a + h) − f(a))/h, so the new value of a changed quantity is about its original value plus the rate of change times the interval of change, f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)h: the y-coordinate at a + h on the tangent line at a.

concepts.name: Velocity
concepts.statement: For a function s(t) giving the position of an object at time t, the velocity of the object at time t is v(t) = s′(t), the rate of change of position.

concepts.name: Speed
concepts.statement: The speed of an object at time t is the absolute value, or magnitude, of its velocity, |v(t)|.

concepts.name: Acceleration
concepts.statement: The acceleration of an object at time t is the rate of change of its velocity, a(t) = v′(t) = s″(t).

concepts.name: Direction and speeding up
concepts.statement: A particle moves in the positive direction where v(t) > 0 and in the negative direction where v(t) < 0, is at rest where v(t) = 0, and is slowing down where velocity and acceleration act in opposite directions, speeding up where they act in the same direction.

concepts.name: Population growth rate
concepts.statement: If P(t) is the number of entities present in a population, the population growth rate of P(t) is its derivative P′(t), the rate of change of the population with respect to time.

concepts.name: Marginal cost
concepts.statement: If C(x) is the cost of producing x items, the marginal cost is MC(x) = C′(x), approximately C(x + 1) − C(x), the cost of producing one more item.

concepts.name: Marginal revenue
concepts.statement: If R(x) is the revenue obtained from selling x items, the marginal revenue is MR(x) = R′(x), approximately the revenue obtained by selling one more item.

concepts.name: Marginal profit
concepts.statement: If P(x) = R(x) − C(x) is the profit obtained from selling x items, the marginal profit is MP(x) = P′(x) = MR(x) − MC(x), approximately the profit obtained by producing and selling one more item.

concepts.name: Derivatives of sine and cosine
concepts.statement: The derivative of the sine function is the cosine and the derivative of the cosine function is the negative sine.

concepts.name: Derivatives of tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant
concepts.statement: The derivatives of the remaining trigonometric functions, found with the quotient rule from those of sine and cosine, are d/dx tan x = sec²x, d/dx cot x = −csc²x, d/dx sec x = sec x tan x and d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x.

concepts.name: Higher-order derivatives of sine and cosine
concepts.statement: The higher-order derivatives of sin x and cos x follow a repeating pattern of four: sin x, cos x, −sin x, −cos x, sin x, so every fourth derivative of sin x equals sin x.

concepts.name: Chain rule
concepts.statement: Let f and g be functions. For all x in the domain of g for which g is differentiable at x and f is differentiable at g(x), the derivative of the composite function h(x) = f(g(x)) is h′(x) = f′(g(x))g′(x), the derivative of the outer function evaluated at the inner function times the derivative of the inner function; if y is a function of u and u is a function of x, dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx.

concepts.name: Applying the chain rule
concepts.statement: To differentiate h(x) = f(g(x)), identify f(x) and g(x), find f′(x) and evaluate it at g(x), find g′(x), and write h′(x) = f′(g(x))·g′(x), working from the outside function in.

concepts.name: Power rule for composition of functions
concepts.statement: For all values of x for which the derivative is defined, if h(x) = (g(x))ⁿ, then h′(x) = n(g(x))ⁿ⁻¹g′(x).

concepts.name: Chain rule with trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: For all x for which the derivative is defined, the chain rule applied to the trigonometric derivatives gives d/dx sin(g(x)) = cos(g(x))g′(x), d/dx cos(g(x)) = −sin(g(x))g′(x), and likewise for the tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant.

concepts.name: Chain rule for a composition of three functions
concepts.statement: For all values of x for which the function is differentiable, if k(x) = h(f(g(x))), then k′(x) = h′(f(g(x)))f′(g(x))g′(x): the chain rule applied twice, a derivative with three parts.

concepts.name: Inverse function theorem
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be a function that is both invertible and differentiable, and y = f⁻¹(x) its inverse. For all x satisfying f′(f⁻¹(x)) ≠ 0, the derivative of the inverse is (f⁻¹)′(x) = 1/f′(f⁻¹(x)); if y = g(x) is the inverse of f(x), then g′(x) = 1/f′(g(x)).

concepts.name: Power rule with rational exponents
concepts.statement: The power rule may be extended to rational exponents: if n is a positive integer, d/dx x^{1/n} = (1/n)x^{(1/n)−1}, and if also m is an arbitrary integer, d/dx x^{m/n} = (m/n)x^{(m/n)−1}.

concepts.name: Derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: The derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions are algebraic: d/dx sin⁻¹x = 1/√(1 − x²), d/dx cos⁻¹x = −1/√(1 − x²), d/dx tan⁻¹x = 1/(1 + x²), d/dx cot⁻¹x = −1/(1 + x²), d/dx sec⁻¹x = 1/(|x|√(x² − 1)) and d/dx csc⁻¹x = −1/(|x|√(x² − 1)).

concepts.name: Implicitly defined function
concepts.statement: If y is expressed entirely in terms of x, y is an explicit function of x; if the relationship is expressed by an equation where y is not expressed entirely in terms of x, the equation defines y implicitly, and in general an equation defines a function implicitly if the function satisfies that equation.

concepts.name: Implicit differentiation
concepts.statement: Implicit differentiation computes dy/dx for a function defined by an equation: differentiate both sides, treating y as a function of x and using the chain rule, move the terms containing dy/dx to the left and the rest to the right, factor out dy/dx and solve for it.

concepts.name: Derivative of bˣ
concepts.statement: On the assumption that B(x) = bˣ, b > 0, is continuous and differentiable at 0, B(x) is differentiable everywhere and its derivative is B′(x) = bˣB′(0).

concepts.name: The number e by its tangent slope
concepts.statement: The number e is the unique value of b > 0 for which B(x) = bˣ has B′(0) = 1: the tangent line to eˣ at x = 0 has slope 1, and 2.7182 < e < 2.7183.

concepts.name: Derivative of the natural exponential function
concepts.statement: Let E(x) = eˣ be the natural exponential function. Then E′(x) = eˣ, and in general d/dx(e^{g(x)}) = e^{g(x)}g′(x).

concepts.name: Derivative of the natural logarithmic function
concepts.statement: If x > 0 and y = ln x, then dy/dx = 1/x; more generally, for a differentiable g(x) and all x with g(x) > 0, the derivative of h(x) = ln(g(x)) is h′(x) = g′(x)/g(x).

concepts.name: Derivatives of general exponential and logarithmic functions
concepts.statement: Let b > 0, b ≠ 1, and g(x) be differentiable. If y = log_b x, then dy/dx = 1/(x ln b), and h(x) = log_b(g(x)) has h′(x) = g′(x)/(g(x) ln b) where g(x) > 0; if y = bˣ, then dy/dx = bˣ ln b, and h(x) = b^{g(x)} has h′(x) = b^{g(x)}g′(x) ln b.

concepts.name: Logarithmic differentiation
concepts.statement: To differentiate y = h(x) by logarithmic differentiation, take the natural logarithm of both sides, expand ln(h(x)) with the properties of logarithms, differentiate both sides implicitly, multiply by y to solve for dy/dx, and replace y by h(x); it differentiates any function g(x)^{f(x)} and simplifies complicated derivatives.

concepts.name: Power rule for real exponents
concepts.statement: For y = xʳ, where r is an arbitrary real number, logarithmic differentiation gives dy/dx = rxʳ⁻¹.

concepts.name: Related rates
concepts.statement: If two related quantities are changing over time, the rates at which the quantities change are related: when a balloon is filled with air, dV/dt and dr/dt are related rates because the volume V is related to the radius r.

concepts.name: Solving a related-rates problem
concepts.statement: To solve a related-rates problem, assign symbols to all variables and draw a figure, state the information given and the rate to be determined, find an equation relating the variables, differentiate both sides with respect to the independent variable using the chain rule, and only then substitute the known values and solve for the unknown rate.

concepts.name: Linear approximation
concepts.statement: For a function f differentiable at a, the linear function L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a), whose graph is the tangent line to f at a, is the linear approximation of f at x = a, also called the tangent line approximation or linearization of f at a; for x near a, f(x) ≈ L(x).

concepts.name: Differential
concepts.statement: For a differentiable function y = f(x), the differential dx is an independent variable that can be assigned any nonzero real number, and the differential dy is defined to be dy = f′(x)dx; the equation dy = f′(x)dx is the differential form of the derivative of y with respect to x.

concepts.name: Approximating change with differentials
concepts.statement: If x changes from a to a + dx, the differential dy = f′(a)dx, the change in y along the tangent line, approximates the actual change Δy = f(a + dx) − f(a) in y, and the approximation is better the closer dx is to zero.

concepts.name: Propagated error
concepts.statement: The propagated error is the error in a calculated quantity f(x) that results from a measurement error dx in x; it can be estimated by dy ≈ f′(x)dx.

concepts.name: Relative error
concepts.statement: Given an absolute error Δq for a particular quantity q, the relative error is Δq/q, the error as a fraction of the quantity.

concepts.name: Percentage error
concepts.statement: The percentage error is the relative error expressed as a percentage, 100 Δq/q.

concepts.name: Absolute extremum
concepts.statement: Let f be a function defined over an interval I and c ∈ I. f has an absolute maximum on I at c if f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x ∈ I, and an absolute minimum on I at c if f(c) ≤ f(x) for all x ∈ I; either one is an absolute extremum on I at c.

concepts.name: Extreme Value Theorem
concepts.statement: If f is a continuous function over the closed, bounded interval [a, b], then there is a point in [a, b] at which f has an absolute maximum over [a, b] and a point in [a, b] at which f has an absolute minimum over [a, b].

concepts.name: Local extremum
concepts.statement: A function f has a local maximum at c if there is an open interval I containing c, contained in the domain of f, with f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x ∈ I, and a local minimum at c if f(c) ≤ f(x) for all x ∈ I; either one is a local extremum at c.

concepts.name: Critical point
concepts.statement: Let c be an interior point in the domain of f. c is a critical number of f if f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) is undefined, and the point (c, f(c)) is a critical point of f; the two terms are often used interchangeably.

concepts.name: Fermat’s theorem
concepts.statement: If f has a local extremum at c and f is differentiable at c, then f′(c) = 0: a local extremum occurs at a critical point.

concepts.name: Location of absolute extrema
concepts.statement: Let f be a continuous function over a closed, bounded interval I. The absolute maximum and the absolute minimum of f over I must occur at endpoints of I or at critical points of f in I.

concepts.name: Locating absolute extrema over a closed interval
concepts.statement: For a continuous function f over [a, b], evaluate f at the endpoints a and b, find the critical points of f in (a, b) and evaluate f there, and compare: the largest value is the absolute maximum of f and the smallest the absolute minimum.

concepts.name: Rolle’s theorem
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over the closed interval [a, b] and differentiable over the open interval (a, b) with f(a) = f(b). Then there exists at least one c ∈ (a, b) such that f′(c) = 0.

concepts.name: Mean Value Theorem
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over [a, b] and differentiable over (a, b). Then there exists at least one point c ∈ (a, b) at which the slope of the tangent line equals the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)): f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).

concepts.name: Functions with a derivative of zero
concepts.statement: Let f be differentiable over an interval I. If f′(x) = 0 for all x ∈ I, then f(x) is constant for all x ∈ I.

concepts.name: Constant difference theorem
concepts.statement: If f and g are differentiable over an interval I and f′(x) = g′(x) for all x ∈ I, then f(x) = g(x) + C for some constant C.

concepts.name: Increasing and decreasing functions corollary
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over [a, b] and differentiable over (a, b). If f′(x) > 0 for all x ∈ (a, b), then f is an increasing function over [a, b]; if f′(x) < 0 for all x ∈ (a, b), then f is a decreasing function over [a, b].

concepts.name: First derivative test
concepts.statement: Suppose f is continuous over an interval I containing a critical point c and differentiable over I except possibly at c. If f′ changes sign from positive to negative as x increases through c, f(c) is a local maximum of f; if from negative to positive, f(c) is a local minimum; if f′ has the same sign on both sides of c, f(c) is neither.

concepts.name: Using the first derivative test
concepts.statement: To find the local extrema of a function f continuous over an interval I, divide I at the critical points of f (and at any point where f′ is discontinuous), find the sign of f′ in each subinterval from a test point, and read from the first derivative test whether f has a local maximum, a local minimum or neither at each critical point.

concepts.name: Concavity
concepts.statement: Let f be differentiable over an open interval I. If f′ is increasing over I, f is concave up over I; if f′ is decreasing over I, f is concave down over I. Concavity is the upward or downward curve of the graph of a function.

concepts.name: Test for concavity
concepts.statement: Let f be twice differentiable over an interval I. If f″(x) > 0 for all x ∈ I, then f is concave up over I; if f″(x) < 0 for all x ∈ I, then f is concave down over I.

concepts.name: Inflection point
concepts.statement: If f is continuous at a and f changes concavity at a, the point (a, f(a)) is an inflection point of f.

concepts.name: Second derivative test
concepts.statement: Suppose f′(c) = 0 and f″ is continuous over an interval containing c. If f″(c) > 0, f has a local minimum at c; if f″(c) < 0, f has a local maximum at c; if f″(c) = 0, the test is inconclusive.

concepts.name: Limit at infinity
concepts.statement: If the values of f(x) become arbitrarily close to L as x becomes sufficiently large, f has a limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L; if they become arbitrarily close to L for x < 0 as |x| becomes sufficiently large, f has a limit at negative infinity, lim_{x→−∞} f(x) = L.

concepts.name: Horizontal asymptote
concepts.statement: If lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L or lim_{x→−∞} f(x) = L, the line y = L is a horizontal asymptote of f; unlike a vertical asymptote, a horizontal asymptote may be crossed, even an unlimited number of times.

concepts.name: Infinite limit at infinity
concepts.statement: A function f has an infinite limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = ∞, if f(x) becomes arbitrarily large for x sufficiently large, and a negative infinite limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = −∞, if f(x) < 0 and |f(x)| becomes arbitrarily large for x sufficiently large; limits as x → −∞ are defined in the same way.

concepts.name: Formal definition of a limit at infinity
concepts.statement: A function f has a limit at infinity if there exists a real number L such that for all ε > 0 there exists N > 0 with |f(x) − L| < ε for all x > N; then lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L. A limit at negative infinity asks for N < 0 and all x < N.

concepts.name: Formal definition of an infinite limit at infinity
concepts.statement: A function f has an infinite limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = ∞, if for all M > 0 there exists an N > 0 such that f(x) > M for all x > N; it has a negative infinite limit at infinity if for all M < 0 there exists N > 0 with f(x) < M for all x > N.

concepts.name: End behavior of rational functions
concepts.statement: For a rational function f(x) = p(x)/q(x), the end behavior is decided by the degrees of p and q: if the degree of p is less than the degree of q, y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote; if they are equal, y = aₙ/bₙ, the ratio of the leading coefficients, is a horizontal asymptote; if the degree of p is greater, f(x) approaches ∞ or −∞ at each end.

concepts.name: Oblique asymptote
concepts.statement: The line y = mx + b is an oblique asymptote of f if f(x) approaches it as x → ∞ or x → −∞; a rational function whose numerator has degree one more than its denominator has one, found by long division.

concepts.name: End behavior of transcendental functions
concepts.statement: sin x and cos x oscillate between −1 and 1 and tan x does not approach a limit or ±∞ as x → ±∞; eˣ approaches ∞ as x → ∞ and 0 as x → −∞, and ln x approaches ∞ as x → ∞.

concepts.name: Drawing the graph of a function
concepts.statement: To sketch the graph of f, determine its domain, its x- and y-intercepts, its end behavior from the limits at ±∞ (a horizontal or an oblique asymptote) and its vertical asymptotes, then find from f′ where f increases and decreases and its local extrema, and from f″ where it is concave up or down and its inflection points.

concepts.name: Optimization problem
concepts.statement: An optimization problem is a problem that is solved by finding the maximum or minimum value of a function, such as maximizing an area or a revenue or minimizing a cost, a time or a surface area.

concepts.name: Solving optimization problems
concepts.statement: To solve an optimization problem, introduce the variables and draw a figure, decide which quantity is to be maximized or minimized, write it as a function of one variable using the equations relating the variables, find the domain the physical problem allows, and locate its maximum or minimum from the critical points and the endpoints, or from the behavior of the function where the interval is open or unbounded.

concepts.name: L’Hôpital’s rule (0/0 case)
concepts.statement: Suppose f and g are differentiable over an open interval containing a, except possibly at a. If lim_{x→a} f(x) = 0 and lim_{x→a} g(x) = 0, then lim_{x→a} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{x→a} f′(x)/g′(x), assuming the limit on the right exists or is ∞ or −∞; it also holds for one-sided limits and for a = ±∞.

concepts.name: L’Hôpital’s rule (∞/∞ case)
concepts.statement: Suppose f and g are differentiable over an open interval containing a, except possibly at a, and lim_{x→a} f(x) and lim_{x→a} g(x) are each ∞ or −∞. Then lim_{x→a} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{x→a} f′(x)/g′(x), assuming the limit on the right exists or is ∞ or −∞; it also holds for a = ±∞ and for one-sided limits.

concepts.name: Indeterminate forms
concepts.statement: When evaluating a limit, the forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰ and 1^∞ are indeterminate: each has no meaning on its own, and further analysis is required to determine whether the limit exists and, if so, what its value is.

concepts.name: Evaluating indeterminate products and differences
concepts.statement: A limit of the form 0·∞ is rewritten as a quotient, f(x)g(x) = f(x)/(1/g(x)), and one of the form ∞ − ∞ is combined over a common denominator or otherwise rewritten, so that it takes the form 0/0 or ∞/∞ and L’Hôpital’s rule applies.

concepts.name: Evaluating indeterminate powers
concepts.statement: For a limit of f(x)^{g(x)} of the form 1^∞, ∞⁰ or 0⁰, take the natural logarithm, y = f(x)^{g(x)} giving ln y = g(x) ln f(x), find the limit of ln y as an indeterminate product, and since lim ln y = L gives lim y = e^L by continuity, the limit is e^L.

concepts.name: Growth rates of functions
concepts.statement: Suppose f and g approach infinity as x → ∞. g grows more rapidly than f as x → ∞ if lim_{x→∞} g(x)/f(x) = ∞, or equivalently lim_{x→∞} f(x)/g(x) = 0; if lim_{x→∞} f(x)/g(x) = M for some constant M ≠ 0, f and g grow at the same rate.

concepts.name: Growth of exponential and logarithmic functions
concepts.statement: The exponential function eˣ grows more rapidly than any power function xᵖ, p > 0, and the logarithmic function ln x grows more slowly than any power function xᵖ, p > 0, as x → ∞.

concepts.name: Newton’s method
concepts.statement: Newton’s method approximates a root of f(x) = 0: from an initial guess x₀ near the root, each approximation is the x-intercept of the tangent line to f at the one before, xₙ = xₙ₋₁ − f(xₙ₋₁)/f′(xₙ₋₁), and the numbers x₀, x₁, x₂, … typically approach the root.

concepts.name: Failures of Newton’s method
concepts.statement: Newton’s method fails when the list x₀, x₁, x₂, … does not approach a finite value or approaches a root other than the one sought: when f′(xₙ) = 0 for some n, when the initial guess is too far from the root, or when the approximations cycle between values.

concepts.name: Iterative process
concepts.statement: An iterative process generates a list of numbers x₀, x₁, x₂, x₃, … by starting with a number x₀ and defining xₙ = F(xₙ₋₁) for n ≥ 1 for some function F; Newton’s method is the iterative process with F(x) = x − f(x)/f′(x).

concepts.name: Cycles and chaos of an iterative process
concepts.statement: An iterative process may converge to a fixed point, bounce between values in a 2-cycle, 4-cycle or longer cycle, or behave chaotically, its values never settling and highly sensitive to the starting number; a cobweb diagram shows which.

concepts.name: Antiderivative
concepts.statement: A function F is an antiderivative of the function f if F′(x) = f(x) for all x in the domain of f; finding an antiderivative reverses differentiation.

concepts.name: General form of an antiderivative
concepts.statement: Let F be an antiderivative of f over an interval I. For each constant C, F(x) + C is also an antiderivative of f over I, and every antiderivative G of f over I is G(x) = F(x) + C for some constant C: the family of antiderivatives F(x) + C is the most general antiderivative of f.

concepts.name: Indefinite integral
concepts.statement: Given a function f, the indefinite integral of f, ∫f(x)dx, is the most general antiderivative of f: if F is an antiderivative of f, then ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C. f(x) is the integrand and x the variable of integration.

concepts.name: Power rule for integrals
concepts.statement: For n ≠ −1, ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C.

concepts.name: Properties of indefinite integrals
concepts.statement: Let F and G be antiderivatives of f and g and k any real number. Then ∫(f(x) ± g(x))dx = F(x) ± G(x) + C and ∫kf(x)dx = kF(x) + C: an indefinite integral of a sum, difference or constant multiple is found term by term.

concepts.name: Differential equation
concepts.statement: A differential equation is an equation that relates an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives; the solutions of dy/dx = f(x) are the antiderivatives of f.

concepts.name: Initial-value problem
concepts.statement: An initial-value problem asks for a function y that satisfies a differential equation dy/dx = f(x) together with an initial condition y(x₀) = y₀; it is solved by finding the family of antiderivatives of f and then the one that satisfies the initial condition.

concepts.name: Method of exhaustion
concepts.statement: Archimedes' method of exhaustion fills an irregular region with smaller and smaller shapes whose areas can be calculated exactly, such as rectangles and triangles, and sums their areas to obtain closer and closer approximations to the total area.

concepts.name: Sigma notation
concepts.statement: Sigma notation, also called summation notation, writes a long sum compactly: the Greek capital letter Σ indicates addition of the terms aᵢ, and the values of the index i below and above the sigma indicate where to begin the summation and where to end it. The index is a dummy variable, used only to keep track of the terms.

concepts.name: Properties of sigma notation
concepts.statement: For sequences of terms aᵢ and bᵢ, a constant c, every positive integer n and every integer m with 1 ≤ m ≤ n: a sum of n copies of c is nc; a constant factor comes out of a sum; the sum of a sum or a difference is the sum or difference of the sums; and a sum splits into the sum of its first m terms and the sum of the rest.

concepts.name: Sums and powers of integers
concepts.statement: The sum of the first n integers is n(n + 1)/2, the sum of their squares is n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, and the sum of their cubes is n²(n + 1)²/4.

concepts.name: Partition
concepts.statement: A partition of [a, b] is a set of points P = {xᵢ}, a = x₀ < x₁ < ⋯ < xₙ = b, that divides the interval into the subintervals [x₀, x₁], [x₁, x₂], …, [xₙ₋₁, xₙ].

concepts.name: Regular partition
concepts.statement: A regular partition of [a, b] is a partition whose subintervals all have the same width, Δx = (b − a)/n, so that xᵢ = x₀ + iΔx.

concepts.name: Left-endpoint approximation
concepts.statement: On each subinterval [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] of a regular partition of [a, b], build a rectangle of width Δx whose height is the function value f(xᵢ₋₁) at the left endpoint; the sum Lₙ of the areas of these n rectangles approximates the area A under the curve.

forms.latex: A\approx L_n=f(x_0)\Delta x+f(x_1)\Delta x+\cdots+f(x_{n-1})\Delta x=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(x_{i-1})\Delta x

concepts.name: Right-endpoint approximation
concepts.statement: On each subinterval [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] of a regular partition of [a, b], build a rectangle of width Δx whose height is the function value f(xᵢ) at the right endpoint; the sum Rₙ of the areas of these n rectangles approximates the area A under the curve.

forms.latex: A\approx R_n=f(x_1)\Delta x+f(x_2)\Delta x+\cdots+f(x_n)\Delta x=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(x_i)\Delta x

concepts.name: Riemann sum
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be defined on a closed interval [a, b] and let P be a regular partition of [a, b] with subintervals of width Δx; for each i let xᵢ* be any point in [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ]. The Riemann sum for f(x) is the sum of the f(xᵢ*)Δx, an estimate of the area under the curve; left- and right-endpoint approximations are Riemann sums.

concepts.name: Upper sum
concepts.statement: An upper sum is a Riemann sum whose sample points xᵢ* are chosen so that f(xᵢ*) is the maximum value of f on each subinterval; it overestimates the area under the curve.

concepts.name: Lower sum
concepts.statement: A lower sum is a Riemann sum whose sample points xᵢ* are chosen so that f(xᵢ*) is the minimum value of f on each subinterval; it underestimates the area under the curve.

concepts.name: Area under the curve
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be a continuous, nonnegative function on [a, b]. The area under the curve y = f(x) on [a, b] is the limit of its Riemann sums as the number n of subintervals goes to infinity; for continuous f the limit exists and does not depend on the choice of the points xᵢ*.

concepts.name: Definite integral
concepts.statement: If f(x) is a function defined on [a, b], the definite integral of f from a to b is the limit of its Riemann sums as n goes to infinity, provided the limit exists. It generalizes the area under a curve to functions that need be neither continuous nor nonnegative; a definite integral is a number, where an indefinite integral is a family of functions.

concepts.name: Integrable function
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is integrable on [a, b], an integrable function, if the limit of its Riemann sums that defines the definite integral exists.

concepts.name: Limits of integration
concepts.statement: The limits of integration are the numbers a and b written below and above the integral sign, the x-values bounding the interval [a, b] over which the function is integrated: a is the lower limit and b the upper limit.

concepts.name: Integrand
concepts.statement: The integrand is the function f(x) written to the right of the integral sign, the function being integrated.

concepts.name: Variable of integration
concepts.statement: The variable of integration is the variable that dx (or dt, du) names after the integrand, the variable the function is integrated with respect to; like the index of a sum it is a dummy variable and any letter may be used.

concepts.name: Continuous functions are integrable
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b], then f is integrable on [a, b]. Functions continuous on a closed interval apart from a finite number of jump discontinuities are integrable too.

concepts.name: Net signed area
concepts.statement: For an integrable function f on [a, b], with A₁ the area between f and the x-axis above the axis and A₂ the area below it, the net signed area A₁ − A₂ is the definite integral of f; it can be positive, negative or zero.

concepts.name: Total area
concepts.statement: The total area between an integrable function f and the x-axis on [a, b] adds the area A₁ above the axis and the area A₂ below it; it is the definite integral of |f(x)|.

concepts.name: Displacement from velocity
concepts.statement: If v(t) is the velocity of an object, the net signed area under its graph over a time interval, the definite integral of v(t), is the object's net displacement, taking direction into account; the integral of |v(t)| is the total distance traveled regardless of direction.

concepts.name: Properties of the definite integral
concepts.statement: An integral with equal limits is 0; reversing the limits changes the integral's sign; the integral of a sum or a difference is the sum or difference of the integrals; a constant factor comes out of the integral; and the integral over [a, b] is the integral over [a, c] plus the integral over [c, b], for all a, b and c, provided f is integrable on the largest interval.

concepts.name: Comparison theorem for integrals
concepts.statement: For a ≤ b: if f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b] its integral is at least 0; if f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b] the integral of f is at least the integral of g; and if m ≤ f(x) ≤ M on [a, b] for constants m and M, the integral lies between m(b − a) and M(b − a).

concepts.name: Average value of a function
concepts.statement: For f(x) continuous on [a, b], the average value of the function, f_ave, is the definite integral of f over [a, b] divided by the length b − a of the interval: the limit of the averages of n sampled values of f.

concepts.name: Mean Value Theorem for Integrals
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous over [a, b], then there is at least one point c in [a, b] at which f takes its average value over [a, b]: f(c) times b − a is the integral of f over [a, b].

concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous over [a, b] and F(x) is the integral of f(t) from a to x, then F′(x) = f(x) over (a, b): the definite integral with a variable upper limit is an antiderivative of its integrand, so every continuous function has an antiderivative.

concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2
concepts.statement: If f is continuous over [a, b] and F(x) is any antiderivative of f(x), then the integral of f over [a, b] is F(b) − F(a): a definite integral is evaluated by evaluating an antiderivative of the integrand at the endpoints of the interval and subtracting, written F(x) evaluated from a to b.

concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
concepts.statement: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, central to the entire development of calculus, establishes the relationship between differentiation and integration in two parts: the first makes a definite integral with a variable limit an antiderivative, and the second evaluates definite integrals with antiderivatives.

concepts.name: Net change theorem
concepts.statement: The new value of a changing quantity F equals its initial value plus the integral of its rate of change F′; equivalently, the integral of F′ over [a, b] is the net change F(b) − F(a), which can be positive, negative or zero.

concepts.name: Integrals of even and odd functions
concepts.statement: For a continuous even function, f(−x) = f(x), the integral over [−a, a] is twice the integral over [0, a]; for a continuous odd function, f(−x) = −f(x), the integral over [−a, a] is 0, since the areas above and below the x-axis are equal.

concepts.name: Substitution with indefinite integrals
concepts.statement: Let u = g(x), where g′(x) is continuous over an interval, let f(x) be continuous over the corresponding range of g, and let F(x) be an antiderivative of f(x). Then the integral of f(g(x))g′(x) dx is the integral of f(u) du, which is F(u) + C = F(g(x)) + C.

concepts.name: Change of variables
concepts.statement: A change of variables is the substitution of a variable, such as u, for an expression in the integrand, and of du for the matching differential, to obtain an expression that is easier to integrate.

concepts.name: Integration by substitution
concepts.statement: To integrate by substitution: select an expression g(x) of the integrand whose derivative g′(x) is also part of it; substitute u = g(x) and du = g′(x) dx, adjusting constants as needed; evaluate the integral in u, or go back and choose another u if it cannot be evaluated; and write the result in terms of x. It finds antiderivatives of integrands that are the result of a chain-rule derivative.

concepts.name: Substitution with definite integrals
concepts.statement: Let u = g(x), let g′ be continuous over [a, b], and let f be continuous over the range of u = g(x). Then the integral of f(g(x))g′(x) from a to b is the integral of f(u) from g(a) to g(b): changing variables changes the limits of integration too.

concepts.name: Integrals of exponential functions
concepts.statement: The exponential function eˣ is its own integral, ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C, and for a base a > 0, a ≠ 1, ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C.

concepts.name: Integration formulas involving logarithmic functions
concepts.statement: The integral of x⁻¹ is the natural logarithm of the absolute value, ∫x⁻¹ dx = ln|x| + C; ∫ln x dx = x ln x − x + C; and ∫log_a x dx = (x/ln a)(ln x − 1) + C.

concepts.name: Price–demand function
concepts.statement: A price–demand function p(x) gives the price of a product at which a quantity x of it is demanded; in general, price decreases as quantity demanded increases.

concepts.name: Marginal price–demand function
concepts.statement: The marginal price–demand function p′(x) is the derivative of the price–demand function; it tells how fast the price changes at a given level of production, and integrating it recovers the price–demand function.

concepts.name: Integrals resulting in inverse trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: For a > 0: ∫du/√(a² − u²) = sin⁻¹(u/a) + C, ∫du/(a² + u²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(u/a) + C, and ∫du/(u√(u² − a²)) = (1/a) sec⁻¹(|u|/a) + C; the other three inverse trigonometric functions give the same integrals with a minus sign.

concepts.name: Area between two curves
concepts.statement: Let f(x) and g(x) be continuous functions such that f(x) ≥ g(x) over an interval [a, b], and let R be the region bounded above by the graph of f(x), below by the graph of g(x), and on the left and right by the lines x = a and x = b. The area of R is the limit of the Riemann sums of rectangles that extend from g(xᵢ*) to f(xᵢ*), the integral of f(x) − g(x) from a to b.

concepts.name: Area between curves that cross
concepts.statement: Let f(x) and g(x) be continuous functions over an interval [a, b] and let R be the region between their graphs, bounded on the left and right by the lines x = a and x = b. The area of R is the integral of |f(x) − g(x)| from a to b; in practice the interval is broken where the graphs cross and an integral is evaluated over each piece.

concepts.name: Finding the area of a compound region
concepts.statement: To find the area of a region whose boundary curves cross or change, find where the graphs intersect, divide the interval there, integrate the upper boundary minus the lower boundary over each piece, and add the areas.

concepts.name: Area between two curves along the y-axis
concepts.statement: Let u(y) and v(y) be continuous functions such that u(y) ≥ v(y) for all y in [c, d], and let R be the region bounded on the right by the graph of u(y), on the left by the graph of v(y), and above and below by the lines y = d and y = c. The area of R is the integral of u(y) − v(y) from c to d, the limit of Riemann sums of horizontal rectangles.

concepts.name: Cross-section
concepts.statement: The cross-section of a solid is the intersection of a plane with the solid.

concepts.name: Cylinder
concepts.statement: A cylinder is any solid that can be generated by translating a plane region along a line perpendicular to the region, called the axis of the cylinder; all its cross-sections perpendicular to the axis are identical, and its volume is the area of the cross-section multiplied by the height of the cylinder.

concepts.name: Slicing method
concepts.statement: To calculate the volume of a solid, slice it into pieces perpendicular to an axis, estimate the volume of each slice by its cross-sectional area times its thickness, and add the estimates; as the number of slices goes to infinity, this Riemann sum becomes the integral of the cross-sectional area A(x) from a to b.

concepts.name: Finding volumes by the slicing method
concepts.statement: Examine the solid and determine the shape of a cross-section, drawing a picture if one is not provided; determine a formula for the area of the cross-section; integrate the area formula over the appropriate interval to get the volume.

concepts.name: Solid of revolution
concepts.statement: A solid of revolution is a solid generated by revolving a region in a plane around a line in that plane.

concepts.name: Disk method
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be continuous and nonnegative and let R be the region bounded above by the graph of f(x), below by the x-axis and on the left and right by the lines x = a and x = b. The volume of the solid of revolution formed by revolving R around the x-axis is the integral of π[f(x)]² from a to b: the slicing method, with circular cross-sections whose area is known ahead of time.

concepts.name: Disk method about the y-axis
concepts.statement: Let g(y) be continuous and nonnegative and let Q be the region bounded on the right by the graph of g(y), on the left by the y-axis, below by the line y = c and above by the line y = d. The volume of the solid of revolution formed by revolving Q around the y-axis is the integral of π[g(y)]² from c to d.

concepts.name: Washer method
concepts.statement: Suppose f(x) and g(x) are continuous, nonnegative functions with f(x) ≥ g(x) over [a, b], and let R be the region between their graphs and the lines x = a and x = b. The volume of the solid formed by revolving R around the x-axis is the integral of π[(f(x))² − (g(x))²] from a to b: its slices are washers, the area of the inner circle subtracted from the area of the outer circle.

concepts.name: Washer method about the y-axis
concepts.statement: Suppose u(y) and v(y) are continuous, nonnegative functions with v(y) ≤ u(y) for y in [c, d], and let Q be the region between their graphs and the lines y = c and y = d. The volume of the solid formed by revolving Q around the y-axis is the integral of π[(u(y))² − (v(y))²] from c to d.

concepts.name: Method of cylindrical shells
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be continuous and nonnegative and let R be the region bounded above by the graph of f(x), below by the x-axis and on the left and right by the lines x = a and x = b. Revolving R around the y-axis turns each rectangle of a partition into a cylindrical shell of volume about 2πxᵢ* f(xᵢ*)Δx, and the volume of the solid is the integral of 2πx f(x) from a to b; about the line x = −k the radius x becomes x + k. The method integrates along the coordinate axis perpendicular to the axis of revolution.

concepts.name: Method of cylindrical shells about the x-axis
concepts.statement: Let g(y) be continuous and nonnegative and let Q be the region bounded on the right by the graph of g(y), on the left by the y-axis, below by the line y = c and above by the line y = d. The volume of the solid formed by revolving Q around the x-axis is the integral of 2πy g(y) from c to d.

concepts.name: Choosing a method for a volume of revolution
concepts.statement: To choose among the disk, washer and shell methods, sketch the region and the solid: disks and washers integrate along the axis parallel to the axis of revolution, washers when the solid has a cavity, and shells along the perpendicular axis, with or without a cavity; take the method whose integral needs the fewest pieces and is easiest to evaluate.

concepts.name: Smooth function
concepts.statement: A function that is differentiable and whose derivative is continuous is called smooth.

concepts.name: Arc length
concepts.statement: The arc length of a curve can be thought of as the distance a person would travel along the path of the curve.

concepts.name: Arc length of a function of x
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be a smooth function over [a, b]. The arc length of the graph of f(x) from (a, f(a)) to (b, f(b)) is the integral of √(1 + [f′(x)]²) from a to b: the limit of the sums of the lengths of line segments joining points of the graph, each segment of length Δx√(1 + [f′(xᵢ*)]²) by the Mean Value Theorem.

concepts.name: Arc length of a function of y
concepts.statement: Let g(y) be a smooth function over a y-interval [c, d]. The arc length of the graph of g(y) from (g(c), c) to (g(d), d) is the integral of √(1 + [g′(y)]²) from c to d.

concepts.name: Surface area
concepts.statement: The surface area of a solid is the total area of the outer layer of the object; for objects such as cubes or bricks, it is the sum of the areas of all of its faces.

concepts.name: Surface of revolution
concepts.statement: A surface of revolution is the surface created by revolving the graph of a function, such as y = f(x) over [a, b], around an axis.

concepts.name: Frustum
concepts.statement: A frustum is a portion of a cone, constructed by cutting the cone with a plane parallel to the base.

concepts.name: Lateral surface area of a frustum
concepts.statement: The lateral surface area of a cone of base radius r and slant height s is πrs; a frustum is a cone with its tip cut off, so its lateral surface area, the lateral surface area of the large cone less that of the small one, is π(r₁ + r₂)l, where r₁ and r₂ are the radii of its wide and narrow ends and l its slant height.

concepts.name: Surface area of a surface of revolution
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be a nonnegative smooth function over [a, b]. The surface area of the surface of revolution formed by revolving the graph of f(x) around the x-axis is the integral of 2πf(x)√(1 + (f′(x))²) from a to b, the limit of the areas of the frustum bands that revolved line segments sweep; for a nonnegative smooth g(y) on [c, d] revolved around the y-axis it is the integral of 2πg(y)√(1 + (g′(y))²) from c to d.

concepts.name: Density function
concepts.statement: A density function describes how mass is distributed throughout an object: a linear density, in mass per unit length; an area density, in mass per unit area, which for a disk may vary only along its radius (a radial density); or a volume density, in mass per unit volume. Weight-density describes weight rather than mass per unit volume.

concepts.name: Mass–density formula of a one-dimensional object
concepts.statement: Given a thin rod oriented along the x-axis over [a, b], with linear density function ρ(x), the mass of the rod is the integral of ρ(x) from a to b, the limit of the sums of the masses ρ(xᵢ*)Δx of its segments.

concepts.name: Mass–density formula of a circular object
